rationale: The student computed 7 + 6 = 13 and wrote '13' directly into the ones place, resulting in 513 instead of regrouping 10 ones into 1 ten. The 'make-a-ten' operation directly models bundling 10 ones into 1 ten and leaving the leftover ones.

script.focus: 10 ones bundling into 1 ten, leaving 4 ones

intent: Demonstrate make-a-ten on the place-value with values [14]. Tutor points at: 10 ones bundling into 1 ten, leaving 4 ones

frames.caption: Here are 14 ones. That is too many for the ones place: it can only hold 0 to 9.
Bundle ten of them. Ten ones make one ten, so the bundle moves to the tens place. 4 ones are left.
Write 1 in the tens place and 4 in the ones place: 14. One digit per place.

judgement.reasoning: The student writes both digits of the ones sum in the ones column (e.g., writing 513 for 37 + 26). This demo directly targets the obstacle by showing 14 ones, explicitly explaining that the ones place can only hold digits 0-9, and demonstrating how bundling 10 ones into 1 ten results in 1 ten and 4 ones (1 in the tens place, 4 in the ones place). It is an easier, prerequisite concept demonstration using a clean worked example.
judgement.verdict: Yes, this demo directly explains why a two-digit sum cannot stay in the ones place and clearly shows how bundling makes 1 ten and leftover ones.
